items.label: text
items.text: Excess means that more than enough acid has been added to react with all the calcium carbonate.

items.label: text
items.text: Calculate the volume (in cm³) of 0.01 g of hydrogen at rtp (A: H = 1). 1 mol H2has a mass of 2g:

items.label: text
items.text: mass number of moles = mass of 1 mol

items.label: formula
items.text: 0 . 0 1 g \, o f \, \text {hydrogen is } \frac { 0 . 0 1 } { 2 } m o l = 0 . 0 0 5 m o l .

items.label: text
items.text: Because we want the volume in cm³ we use the molar volume as 24 000 cm3: volume = number of moles × molar volume

items.label: text
items.text: 0.005 mol of hydrogen occupies 0.005 × 24000 =120 cm³

items.label: text
items.text: You have to be careful that the units are correct when you are calculating a number of moles from a volume. Look carefully, is the volume of gas given in cm³ or dm³? If the volume of the gas is given in cm³ then use the molar volume of the gas as 24 000 cm³, if it is given in dm³ then use 24 dm³.

items.label: text
items.text: Calculate the amount of moles in 120 cm³ of carbon dioxide.

items.label: text
items.text: We can see that the volume is given in cm³ therefore we use 24 000 cm³ as the molar volume:

items.label: text
items.text: volume of gas number of moles = molar volume

items.label: text
items.text: 120 number of moles = 24000

items.label: text
items.text: number of moles = 0.005 mol

items.label: text
items.text: In order to do these calculations, we follow basically the same method as we used for masses in Chapter 5.

items.label: text
items.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced at room temperature and pressure when an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid is added to 1.00g of calcium carbonate. (A: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40; molar volume = 24 dm³ at rtp.)

items.label: text
items.text: The equation for the reaction is

items.label: formula
items.text: C a C O _ { 3 } ( s ) + 2 H C l ( a q ) \rightarrow C a C l _ { 2 } ( a q ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g ) + H _ { 2 } O ( I )

items.label: text
items.text: We have been given the mass of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) and so we can calculate the number of moles of calcium carbonate:

items.label: formula
items.text: n u m b e r o f m o i s = \frac { \ m a s s } { \ m a s s \, o f \, 1 \, m o i }

items.label: text
items.text: The mass of 1 mole of CaCO3 is the M, in grams. The M, is 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100.
